statement: A board has 4 rows and 5 columns of squares. One domino is placed on the board so that it covers exactly two squares that share an edge. In how many different positions can it be placed?

choices.misconception: I only counted the dominoes lying along the rows, 4 in each of the 4 rows, and forgot the upright ones.
I thought every row and every column gives 4 positions, but a column has only 4 squares and so only 3 positions.
I gave every one of the 20 squares two dominoes, one going right and one going down, even for the squares on the right or bottom edge.
I counted from each square to each of its neighbours, which counts every domino twice, once from each end.

hints: Count lying-flat and standing-up positions separately.
A flat domino fits wherever two squares sit side by side in a row. Count the positions in one row, then multiply by the number of rows. Do the same for the columns.
A row of 5 squares has 4 places for a flat domino; a column of 4 squares has 3 places for an upright one.

solutions.reliable: Flat dominoes: each row of 5 squares has 4 places, and there are 4 rows, so there are 16. Upright dominoes: each column of 4 squares has 3 places, and there are 5 columns, so there are 15. In total there are 16 + 15 = 31 positions. The transferable idea: count the positions of a shape by where its first square can go, in each direction separately.
solutions.elegant: Every domino position matches one unit edge shared by two squares. Each of the 4 rows has 4 such edges between its squares, 16 in all, and each of the 3 lines between rows has 5, 15 in all. That makes 31.

whyOnTest: Sliding-window counting tests counting the positions in each direction, rather than cutting the board into pieces or counting each pair twice.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
